title: Council Post: Unlocking SMB Potential: How Generative AI Could Be The Answer
text:
Stephanie Gorski is Strategy Managing Director and Global Strategy Lead for the Software & Platforms Industry at Accenture.
Many people are using generative AI today for digital images and content, and we can already see how generative AI use will expand to shape the future of strategies in nearly every industry.
A recent study from my company, Accenture, found that 97% of global executives believe AI foundation models will enable connections across data types, dramatically changing the ways in which the tool is used. Meanwhile, 98% believe AI foundational models will play an important role in their organizations in the next three to five years.
But could generative AI also be the solution to address the long-standing gap between small- and mid-size businesses (SMBs) and enterprises? SMBs increasingly rely on support from larger businesses. Unfortunately, Accenture’s engagement with these enterprises and SMBs over the last 5+ years has made it clear there is a relationship mismatch between the two groups.
Despite SMBs openly communicating their needs, enterprises have continuously failed to meet them. With the right strategy to address three key SMB challenges, enterprises can enable SMBs to leverage generative AI to drive performance and finally improve the enterprise and SMB relationship.
Increasing Trust: Meeting SMB Needs At Scale
In 2021, Accenture uncovered that 49% of SMBs do not trust the enterprises they work with, despite 83% of enterprises believing otherwise. Two years later, this gap still persists.
SMBs want a tailored experience and want to work with companies that understand their perspectives and can speak their language—this is where enterprises fall short, contributing to diminished trust. Since the same study found that SMBs that trust enterprises spend 5-15% more on products and services, the lack of SMB trust leaves significant revenue on the table.
Generative AI can be leveraged by enterprises to build more trusted relationships with SMBs by offering the more personalized products and services SMBs crave.
A strong first step for enterprises is integrating generative AI into their current products and services—such as Google Workspace bringing AI functionality into commonly used document editors and spreadsheets—to help SMBs more easily manage daily tasks.
As SMBs become familiar with the technology, enterprises can provide more powerful AI tools such as CRM and campaign management integrations that help solve a wider range of SMB challenges. Even generative AI tools such as GitHub’s Copilot, which recently introduced ChatGPT capabilities into its platform, can dramatically improve the speed and efficiency of software engineering, enabling custom feature development at a lower cost.
Driving Efficiency: Turbocharging SMB Productivity
One recent report shows that 16% of SMBs (constituting companies employing 1-499 employees) today have fewer than 20 employees, making efficiency crucial. By helping SMBs increase their efficiency, enterprises can build a longer-term relationship with SMBs and broaden SMB buying behavior.
Generative AI can also help SMBs achieve more output with fewer resources. While there are many generative AI productivity use cases, leaders should focus on providing intuitive AI tools that free up SMBs from repetitive tasks or enable them to accomplish new tasks previously beyond their technical capabilities.
For instance, plugins are now available for ChatGPT that enable interaction with third-party applications, allowing the chatbot to act as an executive assistant while saving the owner both time and resources.
Igniting Growth: Attracting And Retaining Customers
Maintaining and increasing the customer base is a goal that both SMBs and enterprises share, but while SMBs have indicated that retaining current customers is their greatest challenge, newer SMBs see gaining new customers as their largest obstacle.
The more customers SMBs have, the more products and services they will purchase from the enterprise in order to support those customers, leading to mutual growth.
Enterprises can help retain current and convert new customers by optimizing and analyzing customer data for better decision making. This also helps SMBs to better understand their customers, provide higher levels of customer service and create personalized customer messaging and experiences.
Generative AI holds strong potential to continue to push the possibilities of customer success even further, helping SMBs quickly scale capabilities to reach new customers and markets through personalized interactions and campaigns.
Strategies For SMBs Looking To Integrate AI Solutions: A Case Example
Imagine a local sports outfitter that operates entirely online and relies on an enterprise platform for its e-commerce and technology needs. When looking to grow its business, this small business can leverage a generative AI analytics tool to identify high-potential, untapped markets.
This tool then creates a fully formed marketing plan and personalized ad messaging, specifically designed for each customer segment. The owner also creates a 30-second, cinematic promotional video using an AI image and video generator in under an hour without needing deep technical skills.
With the influx of new customers, the sports outfitter experiences a setback with a recall on a popular product, driving a huge increase in customer service call volume. As the lean team struggles to respond to all the inquiries, they deploy a generative AI-powered customer support tool.
These tools can field all calls simultaneously using an AI chatbot agent that knows the entire customer profile, monitors ongoing caller sentiment, speaks in an appropriate tone and offers additional product recommendations based on purchase history and interests.
This conversation is indistinguishable from speaking with a real human, providing that personal attention customers expect from small businesses.
Generative AI can allow such an SMB to scale their operations beyond what was previously possible—and would be because of the enterprise that took the steps to unlock generative AI for this SMB.
Generative AI Transforming The Enterprise And SMB Relationship
Enterprises have long wrestled with how to engage SMBs in the way they need while being conscious of the resources it takes to deliver such service.
I hope this article offers some valuable takeaways for enterprise leaders seeking to offer SMBs the support they need by focusing on ways to provide trusted, personalized, easy-to-use products and services which can allow both parties to reach new heights.

title: Council Post: ChatGPT Is Revolutionary—But Maybe Not In The Way You Think
text:
Robert Napoli is the CEO of Agile Tech Advisors. He writes about cybersecurity, digital transformation and tech leadership.
When OpenAI released GPT-2, journalists were blown away.
“Give it a fake headline, and it’ll write the rest of the article,” a writer for The Verge marveled. “Feed it the first line of a short story, and it’ll tell you what happens to your character next. It can even write fan fiction, given the right prompt.”
It could also write jokes and poetry. Some writers remarked that this algorithm might one day steal their jobs, and scientists were already observing scenarios where humans couldn’t reliably distinguish between AI-generated and human art.
However, GPT-2 was released four years ago. So why is everybody talking about AI now, as if something has changed?
The Problem With Older Chatbots
The last decade's most advanced chatbots and translators were built on recurrent neural networks (RNNs), long short-term memory networks (LSTMs) and other machine learning algorithms that processed language in sequential order.
They were great but limited. In the time they took to train, the labor involved in labeling huge datasets and, most notably, their ability to handle longer sentences and passages of text. After all, reading, writing and translating require memory—the first part of this sentence, paragraph and article have a bearing on those written here—and those sequential models weren't cutting it in that department due to the vanishing gradient problem.
We needed a new way to teach AI to do things—not just a bigger or more fine-tuned model, but something characteristically different. That breakthrough—the change that brought us the modern AI we see today—did not occur last November. It happened iteratively, over half a decade ago.
AI's Technological Breakthrough
In 2017, researchers from Google and the University of Toronto had an idea: that all you really need is attention.
Consider where your attention is focused now: on these words you’re reading, on the operative idea introduced in the last sentence—attention (what does it mean here?)—and the point of the article (boy, this is a long road to talking about ChatGPT). Through attention, you can retain the context and meaning in this sentence, and the article overall, without having to remember every word or sentence you’ve already read.
Now, what if AI could exhibit attention? This idea enabled those researchers to design what they called a “transformer.”
Unlike RNNs and LTSMs, which processed data sequentially, the transformer could simultaneously handle entire data sequences, using attention as its weapon to make sense of it all. It was more accurate because it didn’t have to put so much effort into remembering every cumulative word that ever came before it. In these and other ways, the transformer was much more like an actual neural network than its predecessors.
And for training purposes, the transformer was a dream. With sequential processing, you could only feed an algorithm as fast as it could consume one data point after another. Without that limitation, transformers could run through gobs of data extremely quickly.
But there was one more problem. “Although large unlabeled text corpora are abundant,” a group of researchers noted in 2018, “labeled data for learning these specific tasks is scarce, making it challenging for discriminatively trained models to perform adequately.” Those researchers were from OpenAI, and their solution was an entirely new, preemptive stage of the standard training process, which didn’t require labeled training data. They called it “generative pre-training,” or GPT.
From there, most of the gains were in scale. The first GPT was built on 117 million parameters, informed by Common Crawl and a collection of over 11,000 books. GPT-2 had ten times the training data with 1.5 billion parameters in all. GPT-3—the one which underpinned the release of the ChatGPT app—was about one hundred times bigger than its predecessor with 175 billion parameters.
As you can see, the most significant technological advancements occurred years before ChatGPT existed. So why is this app important at all?
Because ChatGPT was not a revolution in what AI could do. It was, instead, a revolution in what AI could be.
What ChatGPT Changed
AI has been a part of our lives for some time now. It’s in our phones, the websites we use, the planes we fly in and plenty in between. But these algorithms are all distant—they enable, inform and smooth out the things we interact with, all behind the scenes.
ChatGPT is the world’s first AI tool you can engage with without that buffer. Researchers have been using it for research, students for studying and educators for educating. It has assisted not just executives and managers but their assistants. It can help you develop ideas for almost anything, even prompts to feed other AI tools.
The breakthrough of ChatGPT isn’t technical—it’s democratic. It’s not about how good it is, but how many people can use it freely and in different ways.
And make no mistake: The accessibility of AI is just as important as its technical sophistication.
Late last year, the White House announced a blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights, citing just a few of the many possible negative impacts this technology could have on society: including privacy, racial discrimination, job loss and more. What’s understated is that so many of these problems are rooted not only in what AI can do but who controls it—governments, corporate executives and cybercriminals.
If AI is to be a net positive for society in the long run, it won’t be because it gets so advanced. Instead, it’ll be because everybody can use it to enhance their own lives.
ChatGPT showed us that the real reason we care about AI isn’t just because of how good it is but how good it is for us.
